# IELTS Reading Skills

A short handbook used as an ingestion fixture. The structure matters more than
the prose: two chapters, each with subsections, so the chunker has real joints
to cut at.

## Chapter 1: Skimming for gist

Skimming means reading quickly to find the general idea of a passage. You move
your eyes over the text without stopping on individual words, and you accept
that you will not understand every sentence.

### When to skim

Skim before you read the questions, not after. A candidate who reads the
questions first tends to hunt for words rather than follow the argument, and
matching-headings tasks punish that badly.

### How long to spend

Two minutes for a nine-hundred-word passage is enough. If you are still
skimming after three minutes you are reading, not skimming, and the timing for
the whole paper will suffer.

## Chapter 2: Scanning for detail

Scanning is the opposite movement: you already know what you are looking for,
and you are searching the page for it. Numbers, dates, proper nouns and
capitalised terms are the easiest targets because they stand out visually.

### Choosing the search term

Pick the word in the question least likely to be paraphrased. A date survives
paraphrase; an adjective usually does not. Candidates who scan for a synonym of
the question's verb almost always end up in the wrong paragraph.

### Distractors

Examiners place a plausible wrong answer near the correct one deliberately. If
the first thing you find matches the question exactly, read the sentence before
it and the sentence after it before you commit.

## Chapter 3: Managing the clock

Sixty minutes, three passages, forty questions. That is ninety seconds a
question including the reading, and the third passage is the hardest, so
finishing passage one early is worth more than getting every answer in it.
